documents.title: AI and Honor Code Advice for Faculty
documents.summary: Honor Code office advice to faculty: the university has no one-size-fits-all AI policy, each instructor decides what resources are allowed, and instructors should tell students that AI is unauthorized unless explicitly allowed. It also asks faculty to report suspected misuse to the Honor Council and to point students to a checklist for verifying AI output.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'the individual instructor determines what resources are permitted' and 'The university does not have a one-size-fits-all AI policy', so the decision is handed to instructors and the document sets no stance itself. It adds a fallback ('consider AI to be an unauthorized resource' if not authorized), but that applies only where the instructor is silent, so the document-level stance is delegates.

units.why: The page opens by framing AI as a source of student confusion and asks faculty to stress the points below; this is an institution-level framing statement ('fast-evolving resource that has the potential to create confusion'), so P56 (framework preamble stating purpose) with actor all and phase general; it states no rule, so informs/neutral.
units.anchor: AI is a fast-evolving resource that has the potential to create confusion among students.
units.fit_note: Preamble naming student confusion as the reason for the guidance, rather than a full framework of principles.

units.why: Tells faculty to emphasize the listed points to students: 'We encourage you to emphasize the following points in your guidance to students'. This is advice to instructors on explaining AI rules to students, so P66 (explain rules), instructor, course-start, should.

documents.title: AIPI Final Report
documents.summary: A task-force report to the Provost with recommendations (not adopted policy) on AI in teaching, literacy, research, operations, security and IP. It recommends mandatory AI statements in syllabi, a flexible framework that keeps faculty and unit discretion, Honor Code clarification, and a new AI council; appendices hold sample syllabus tiers and integrity frameworks.

It sets no single AI stance for coursework, and its appendix offers tiers of use, so the stance is delegates.

documents.title: Honor Code Sample Syllabus Language
documents.summary: Sample syllabus language from the Honor Code office. Instructors fill in which aids, including AI, they allow; the default is that anything not expressly permitted is not allowed, and AI is named among the aids barred on exams.
documents.stance_why: The template asks the instructor to 'Begin by informing students as to what you do permit' and to be specific about whether students can use AI, so the choice is left to the instructor. The default 'assume it is not permitted' applies only if the instructor gives no permission, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: The template line 'Begin by informing students as to what you do permit' directs instructors to say in the syllabus which aids, 'for example ... AI', are permitted, so P09 (syllabus statement); instructor, course-start, should.
units.anchor: Begin by informing students as to what you do permit

units.why: Model syllabus text 'Unless I have provided express permission to use an outside resource, assume it is not permitted' sets a fallback when permission is silent (P06); the aid list explicitly names AI. Student, course-start, should (assume), restrict.

notes: Coder B. The AIPI report is a set of recommendations, not adopted policy; units from its appendices summarising other universities' practice were mostly skipped, and only statements the report itself endorses were coded. Navigation and site boilerplate skipped. Non-AI honor-code text in the model syllabus skipped. Absence statements (no university-wide policy) were coded UNCOVERED.
